title: Why does the Pacific coast almost never thunder?
teaches: Why does Florida hear thunder ninety days a year while the coast from Seattle to San Francisco hears it on only a handful? A cold summer sea, a strong inversion lid from sinking air aloft, the marine layer pulled inland by hot valleys, and the rare winter days when the coast does thunder.

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: The ocean off the West Coast stays cold even in August, chilled by the **California Current** from the Gulf of Alaska and by summer north winds that drive cold water up from the depths (**upwelling**).

Overhead sits the **Pacific High**, a vast zone of sinking air. Because sinking air warms as it is compressed, the air a kilometre up is much warmer than the sea-chilled air beneath it, forming a strong inversion lid.

Trapped beneath that lid is the **marine layer**: a shallow wedge of cool, damp air topped by stratus or stratocumulus. Hot inland valleys pull it onshore during the day and evening, and morning sun burns it back toward the beach.

Thunderstorms require buoyant air parcels that stay warmer than their surroundings all the way past the freezing level. Over a cold sea and under a warm lid, rising air stops after a few hundred metres. Thunderstorms need either a warm sea or cold air aloft.
The Pacific coast’s few thunderstorms happen mostly in autumn and winter, after the summer lid vanishes and cold air from the Gulf of Alaska sweeps over ocean water that is mild by comparison.

blocks.text: Lesson 5 showed how summer sunshine baking damp ground can build a towering thunderstorm by mid-afternoon. Along the Gulf Coast of Florida, that happens on roughly ninety days a year; in Kansas, on about fifty-five. Yet along the Pacific coast from Seattle to San Francisco, thunder is heard on only three to five days a year, and in some years not at all. The coastal air is certainly not short of moisture—summer beaches are famously damp and foggy—so something else must be preventing the clouds from growing tall.

blocks.caption: Approximate number of thunderstorm days per year across the United States, from Florida to the Pacific coast.

options.title: Days a year with thunder, roughly

blocks.text: The first reason lies in the ocean itself. Wade into the surf on the Oregon or northern California coast in August and the water is around 11 to 13 °C (52 to 55 °F)—cold enough to make your ankles ache. Off Florida or the Carolinas in August, the sea surface sits at 28 to 30 °C (82 to 86 °F), as warm as a heated swimming pool. The West Coast sits along the **California Current**, the slow eastern limb of the North Pacific gyre that carries cool subarctic water southward from the Gulf of Alaska. And in summer, the coastal wind makes the water right against the shore colder still.

All summer long, the prevailing wind along the Pacific coast blows from the north or northwest. You might expect a north wind to push the surface water straight south along the beach. As Lesson 9 showed, however, the Earth’s rotation deflects any freely moving fluid to the right of its path in the Northern Hemisphere. When a north wind drags on the ocean surface, the top layer of water actually drifts to the right of the wind—westward, straight out to sea.[^ekman] As that surface layer is skimmed offshore, deep, frigid water (8 to 10 °C) rises from 50 to 100 metres down to replace it along the coast. This process is **coastal upwelling**, and it often makes the ocean at the beach colder in July than it was in April.[^upwelling-life]

blocks.caption: Cross-section of the coast looking north. A north wind blows toward you (out of the page) and drives surface water offshore to the West; a south wind blows away from you.
blocks.task: Try a south wind, then blow a north wind along the coast until the sea at the shore is cold enough to fog the air.

blocks.text: When mild, humid air from the open Pacific (with a dew point around 12 or 13 °C) drifts across that belt of upwelled 10 °C water near the shore, the bottom of the air mass is chilled below its dew point and condenses into sea fog (Lesson 1). Along the West Coast in summer, the air near the surface is cooled from below rather than heated.[^twain]

parts.title: A lid pressed down from above

blocks.text: The second reason sits overhead. Every summer, a massive semi-permanent high-pressure system expands across the eastern North Pacific, centred roughly a thousand kilometres west of San Francisco: the **North Pacific High**. As in every Northern Hemisphere high (Lesson 9), surface winds spiral clockwise outward around it while air aloft slowly sinks to replace them. Along the eastern flank of the high—right against the North American coast—that clockwise circulation blows steadily from north to south, supplying the exact north wind that drives coastal upwelling.

Meanwhile, the air sinking out of the upper levels of the Pacific High compresses as it descends into higher pressure, warming at the dry rate of 10 °C per kilometre and drying out along the way (Lesson 2). That warm, sinking air mass comes to rest directly on top of the shallow layer of air chilled by the cold ocean below. As a result, the air one kilometre above the beach in July is often 10 to 15 °C *warmer* than the air at the sand—a remarkably strong temperature **inversion** sitting just 300 to 800 metres above the sea.

blocks.caption: The North Pacific High in summer seen from above (left), and a vertical slice through the coastal atmosphere showing warm, sinking air capping the cool marine layer (right).

blocks.text: The Pacific High is part of a global circulation belt. Warm, humid air that rises in the deep thunderstorm belts near the equator flows poleward at high altitude and sinks back toward the surface around 30° north and south latitude, forming a ring of **subtropical highs** around the globe.[^belt] Beneath that descending, dry air lie the world’s great hot deserts—the Sahara, the Arabian Desert, the Atacama, and the Kalahari—and on the eastern edges of the ocean basins, it produces dry summers from California to the Mediterranean.

Sandwiched between the cold ocean below and the warm inversion lid above sits the **marine layer**: a shallow slab of cool, moist ocean air only a few hundred metres thick. Gentle mixing by the wind cools the top of this trapped layer to its dew point, forming a persistent deck of **stratus** or **stratocumulus** pressed flat against the base of the inversion (Lesson 2). In coastal California, this late-spring and early-summer overcast is so reliable that locals call it the *June Gloom*.

What pulls this coastal cloud deck onshore and offshore each day is the heating and cooling of the land. Just across the coastal hills, interior valleys like California’s Central Valley or Oregon’s Willamette Valley bake under clear skies to 35 or 40 °C (95 to 105 °F). As hot air rises over the interior, surface pressure falls there, creating a pressure gradient that sucks cool, dense marine air inland through every gap and river gorge in the Coast Ranges—a daily **sea breeze** on a regional scale.[^sf-gaps] After sunset, the inland pull relaxes, but the humid marine air that flowed inland cools overnight until stratus fills the coastal valleys by dawn. After sunrise, sunshine penetrates the thin inland edge of the cloud deck first, warming the ground below and evaporating the stratus back toward the coast by afternoon (Lesson 1). By mid-afternoon, the inland valleys are blazing hot and cloudless while the beach remains cool and grey.

blocks.caption: Daily advance and retreat of the marine layer from the coast into an inland valley through a gap in the coastal hills.
blocks.task: Make the valley hot, then find the afternoon hour when the beach is grey and the valley is clear.

blocks.text: Because the interior heat drives the pressure gradient, the hottest days inland pull the marine layer hardest. When Sacramento hits 40 °C, the sea breeze through the Golden Gate is at its briskest and San Francisco stays wrapped in cold, blowing fog. Where the base of the stratus deck lowers all the way to the waves, the foghorns sound along the headlands.

parts.title: Heat the land, still no storm

blocks.text: Now consider what it takes to build a thunderstorm. As Lesson 5 showed, a thunderstorm grows when a rising parcel of air stays warmer and less dense than the surrounding atmosphere all the way up through the middle troposphere—well past the 0 °C freezing level where ice crystals and soft hail (*graupel*) collide to separate electrical charge.

Over the summer Pacific off Oregon or California, a parcel of air near the water starts out at the temperature of the sea: around 13 or 14 °C. The sounding chart below plots that rising parcel (orange) against the surrounding coastal atmosphere (violet). Test how high the parcel can climb.

blocks.caption: Sounding chart for a parcel rising off the cool Pacific (orange) through the surrounding atmosphere (violet), and the resulting cloud.
blocks.task: Guess first. Then find a sea and an air aloft that build a thunderstorm.

blocks.text: Within 400 to 600 metres of the surface, the rising parcel runs straight into the Pacific High’s inversion lid, where the surrounding air jumps 10 °C warmer. Suddenly much colder and denser than the air around it, the parcel stops dead in its tracks, flattening into shallow stratocumulus thousands of metres below the freezing level.

To punch past a low-level cap and build a thunderstorm, the atmosphere needs either a **much warmer ocean** at the bottom or **much colder air** aloft. Off Florida in August, the ocean surface is 29 °C (84 °F), loading the boundary layer with nearly three times as much water vapour as the cool Pacific air. When a hot, steamy Gulf parcel rises, condensing vapour releases so much latent heat that the parcel stays warmer than the surrounding sky all the way to the tropopause at 12 kilometres. The second way to get a thunderstorm—putting bitter cold air aloft over milder water—is how the Pacific coast gets its rare winter lightning.

What about the hot inland valleys of the West, where summer afternoons regularly top 35 °C? Even there, the sinking air of the Pacific High keeps the middle troposphere warm and bone-dry, so rising thermals often run out of moisture or hit a mid-level cap before reaching the freezing level. Interior western thunderstorms mainly break out when summer monsoon winds import mid-level moisture northward from Mexico and the Gulf of California,[^monsoon] or when an upper-level trough brings unseasonably cold air aloft. Because the air near the ground is still hot and dry, those interior storms often have high bases (3 to 4 km up); much of their rain evaporates on the way down as virga, unleashing **dry lightning** across parched summer forests.

parts.title: The few days it does thunder

blocks.text: When autumn arrives, the North Pacific High weakens and retreats southward toward Hawaii, taking the coastal inversion lid with it, while the polar jet stream dips south to steer Pacific cyclones into Washington, Oregon, and California (Lesson 9). Behind each passing cold front, polar air pours straight down from the Gulf of Alaska, bringing temperatures of −5 °C to −10 °C just 1.5 kilometres above the waves. Yet the ocean water, which changes temperature very slowly through the seasons, still sits at 10 to 12 °C.

Now the summer temperature profile is flipped upside down: instead of cold water under warm air aloft, the coast has **comparatively mild water under frigid air aloft**. Heated and moistened from below by the 11 °C sea, rising air parcels stay warmer than the cold polar air overhead for kilometres, erupting into lines of **cumulus congestus** and small **cumulonimbus** towers. Between October and March, these post-frontal bands march ashore with sudden squalls, heavy downpours, bouncing pellets of soft hail (**graupel**), brief waterspouts offshore, and occasional sharp cracks of thunder.[^winter-lightning] Along the Pacific coast, thunderstorm season is winter—the exact opposite of the continental interior.

So the West Coast is never short of moisture. In summer, it is short of instability: a cold ocean cools the air at the bottom while sinking air in the Pacific High warms the air at the top, locking the marine moisture into a shallow grey sheet.

items.question: The weather forecast calls for the interior Sacramento Valley to hit 40 °C (104 °F) this afternoon. What should you expect this morning and afternoon on the coast at San Francisco?
options: Hot, cloudless beach weather, since all of northern California is under a heat wave
Cool, foggy, and breezy: intense heating in the interior valley lowers surface pressure there, pulling the marine layer and stratus strongly onshore
Severe afternoon thunderstorms along the beach triggered by the inland heat
items.why: Hot air rising in the interior valley lowers surface pressure there, strengthening the onshore pressure gradient. The hotter the interior valley gets, the harder it pulls cool, foggy marine air onshore through coastal gaps like the Golden Gate.

instruments: Wind: north, 35 km/h, for three days
items.question: A brisk north wind (35 km/h) has blown parallel to the Oregon coast for three straight days in July. How has that wind changed the ocean water at the beach and the sky above it?
options: Warmed the surf by blowing summer-heated air off the headlands
Pushed all clouds out to sea and warmed the beach
Cooled the surf to ~10 °C via coastal upwelling (as Coriolis deflection drives surface water offshore) and chilled the damp ocean air into sea fog and low stratus
items.why: In the Northern Hemisphere, a north wind blowing down the coast drives surface water 90° to the right (westward, out to sea) via Ekman transport. Cold deep water wells up along the beach to replace it, chilling the humid marine air to its dew point.

items.question: On a brisk December afternoon behind a Pacific cold front, the ocean surface off Washington is 10 °C while the air 1.5 km overhead is −8 °C. Can a thunderstorm form over the coastal waters today?
options: Yes: an 18 °C temperature drop over 1.5 km (12 °C/km) is strongly unstable, allowing air warmed by the 10 °C sea to build cumulonimbus showers with graupel and thunder
No: the Pacific coast is too cold in December for convective clouds to form
No: the Pacific High’s inversion lid is strongest in December
items.why: Instability depends on the temperature difference between the surface and the air aloft. Dropping 18 °C in 1.5 km (12 °C/km) is steeper than even the dry adiabatic rate (10 °C/km), so air warmed by the 10 °C ocean rises freely into winter cumulonimbus showers.

items.question: On a sunny July afternoon, cumulus clouds are bubbling up over the inland foothills thirty kilometres from the coast, yet right over the beach sits a flat, featureless deck of stratocumulus. Why don't cumulus heaps grow over the beach?
options: The afternoon sea breeze blows the cumulus clouds inland as fast as they form
Air over the cold surf starts out cool (12–14 °C) and hits the warm sinking inversion lid of the Pacific High just a few hundred metres up, stopping vertical growth
There is not enough water vapour over the ocean to feed cumulus clouds
items.why: Convective clouds can only climb while they remain warmer than the surrounding air. Over the cold coastal water, rising air starts cool and immediately runs into the warm subsidence inversion of the Pacific High a few hundred metres up, spreading flat into stratocumulus.

learned: Summer ocean water off the West Coast is cold (10–14 °C), cooled by the southward California Current and by coastal upwelling—where north winds and rightward Coriolis deflection (Ekman transport) drive surface water offshore and draw frigid deep water up to the beach.

Overhead in summer sits the North Pacific High (part of the global 30° latitude belt of subtropical highs). Its sinking air warms by compression at 10 °C/km, creating a strong inversion lid 300 to 800 metres above the cool sea.

Trapped beneath the inversion lid is the cool, damp marine layer, topped by stratus and stratocumulus. Rising hot air in interior valleys pulls the marine layer onshore through coastal gaps, while morning sunlight burns the cloud deck back from its thinner inland edge.

Thunderstorms require buoyant parcels that stay warmer than their surroundings past the freezing level. Over the cold summer Pacific and beneath the warm inversion lid, parcels stop at a few hundred metres—whereas Florida's 29 °C sea fuels deep storms almost daily.

Most of the Pacific coast’s few thunderstorms occur in autumn and winter behind cold fronts, when the summer lid is gone and frigid air from the Gulf of Alaska flows over the comparatively mild (10–11 °C) ocean, triggering convective showers, graupel, and occasional lightning.

upwelling.title: Upwelling
upwelling.text: When summer north winds blow down the Pacific coast, the Earth's rotation (Ekman transport) deflects the surface water 90° to the right—westward, away from the shore. Cold water (8–10 °C) rises from 50–100 metres depth to replace it along the beach, often making the surf colder in July than in April and chilling moist ocean air into sea fog.

pacific-high.title: The Pacific High
pacific-high.text: A vast semi-permanent subtropical high-pressure system over the eastern North Pacific in summer. Its clockwise outflow drives the coastal north winds, while its sinking air warms by compression to clamp a strong temperature inversion 300 to 800 metres above the sea-chilled marine layer.

marine-layer.title: The marine layer
marine-layer.text: A shallow layer of cool, humid air (300–800 m deep) trapped between the cold coastal ocean and the warm subsidence inversion of the Pacific High, usually topped by a flat deck of stratus or stratocumulus. Hot inland valleys draw it onshore via the sea breeze, and daytime sun erodes it from its inland edge.

coast-thunder.title: Thunder on the coast
coast-thunder.text: Summer thunderstorms are virtually absent along the Pacific coast because cool ocean water at the bottom and warm sinking air aloft prevent clouds from growing past a few hundred metres. The coast's few thunderstorms arrive mainly in autumn and winter behind cold fronts, when frigid Gulf of Alaska air aloft passes over 10–11 °C ocean water.

ekman.title: Ekman transport and coastal upwelling
ekman.text: When wind blows across the ocean, surface drag sets the top layer moving while the Coriolis effect continually deflects the moving water to the right (in the Northern Hemisphere). As Vagn Walfrid Ekman showed mathematically in 1902 (following Fridtjof Nansen’s Arctic ice observations), the net transport of the top 50 to 100 metres of wind-driven water—called **Ekman transport**—runs at **90° to the right of the wind direction**. A north wind blowing south along the Oregon and California coast therefore pushes the surface water due west out to sea.

upwelling-life.title: Why cold upwelling water teems with life
upwelling-life.text: Warm sunlit surface waters in the open ocean are often biological deserts because sinking dead organisms carry nitrogen and phosphorus down into the dark depths. Where coastal upwelling pulls deep water back into the sunlit zone—along California and Oregon, Peru, Namibia, and northwest Africa—it acts as a giant fertilizer pump, feeding dense blooms of phytoplankton that support some of the richest sardine, anchovy, salmon, and whale feeding grounds on Earth.

twain.title: Mark Twain and San Francisco’s 'winter'
twain.text: The famous quip *'The coldest winter I ever spent was a summer in San Francisco'* is universally attributed to Mark Twain, though quote researchers have never found it in his letters, notebooks, or books (the closest match in an 1879 letter is Twain recalling a freezing Paris spring). Whoever coined it nailed the climatology: thanks to peak summer upwelling and relentless afternoon fog through the Golden Gate, July and August afternoon highs on the San Francisco coast average just 17–19 °C (63–66 °F), and the city's warmest month of the year is actually September or October, when the Pacific High weakens and upwelling relaxes.

belt.title: The Hadley cell and the 'Horse Latitudes'
belt.text: In 1735, George Hadley proposed that intense solar heating near the equator drives a giant overturning loop in each hemisphere—now called the **Hadley cell**. Air rises in the equatorial thunderstorm belt, flows poleward near the tropopause, and sinks back to the surface around 30° N and 30° S, creating the **subtropical highs** (such as the North Pacific High and the Azores/Bermuda High). Sailing ships becalmed for weeks under the light, sinking winds of these highs named the belt around 30° the **Horse Latitudes**.

sf-gaps.title: Why the Golden Gate is a wind tunnel
sf-gaps.text: California’s Coast Ranges form a continuous wall blocking the 500-metre-deep marine layer from reaching the blazing-hot Central Valley—except at a single sea-level notch: the **Golden Gate** and San Francisco Bay (along with the Petaluma Gap just north). On summer afternoons when Redding and Sacramento bake at 40 °C and San Francisco sits at 15 °C, the resulting pressure gradient funnels a 30 to 50 km/h river of cold marine air and shredded stratus straight across the Golden Gate Bridge toward Berkeley and the Carquinez Strait.

monsoon.title: The North American Monsoon
monsoon.text: From July through early September, intense summer heating over the high plateau of Mexico and the American Southwest reverses the regional upper-level winds, drawing mid-level moisture northward from the Gulf of California and eastern Pacific. This **North American Monsoon** transforms Arizona and New Mexico from bone-dry in May and June to almost daily afternoon thunderstorms in July and August, and occasional moisture surges ride all the way north into eastern Oregon, Idaho, and Washington.

winter-lightning.title: Winter 'superbolts' over cold seas
winter-lightning.text: Although winter thunderstorms over the North Pacific and coastal Washington are shallow—with cloud tops reaching only 5 or 6 km instead of 12 km—the lightning bolts they do fire are often extraordinarily powerful. Because the −10 °C to −20 °C charging zone sits just 1.5 to 2.5 kilometres above the ocean surface in winter, positive charge centres sit much closer to the sea, occasionally discharging massive positive cloud-to-ground strokes ('superbolts') that shake coastal windows for miles.
